utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Before the next witness is brought in, I wanted to just update Your Honours on our witness scheduling this week. We were just informed by Victims and Witnesses Unit -- it's actually right before the court hearing started today that Mr. Brakovic is no longer in hospital. Happily his health condition has improved, and we have been told that he may be available to testify immediately after Mr. Abrahams concludes his testimony. However, I should point out that we have not yet been able to speak to him. We will do that this afternoon in the course of the afternoon, so I will be able -- in a position to give you a more -- or confirm what will happen at the end of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We are glad for the witness, and we are glad that it offers us the prospect of dealing with that witness before the end of the week as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Depending on the progress with Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I also wanted to add, Your Honours, that the two crime base witnesses that we have brought forward in the event that Mr. Brakovic was not going to be available this week, and these are Ms. Hajrizi and Mr. Latifi. We have been able to obtain visas for them and their travel arrangements have been secured. So in the event that Mr. Brakovic is not well enough to testify once Mr. Abrahams concludes his testimony, we will proceed on Thursday with the evidence of Ms. Hajrizi. But again, this is something we will only be able to confirm at the end of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps now Mr. Abrahams can be brought in. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that before the witness is brought in, I would like to deal with some remarks and proposals regarding the testimony of Mr. Fred Abrahams. The Defence would like to object to some portions of Mr. Abrahams's statements because it believes that these are irrelevant, unreliable, or inappropriate for a fact witness. The Defence would like to emphasize that Mr. Abrahams was called here as a fact witness, not as an expert in any field; and that is why we object to the portions of his statement where he, for all intents and purposes, acts as an expert witness. Had he been called here as an expert witness, we would have to operate in accordance with the Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence the Defence contends. The Defence would like to object to Exhibit P386 tendered into evidence by the Prosecution, and that is a report entitled: "Rape as a form of Ethnic Cleansing." We assume on the basis of an analysis of the previous transcripts of this witness and his statements that this document was tendered into evidence to indicate that the Serbian authorities were aware of what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija, that they had been receiving reports, but bearing in mind that this report was published in May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 2000 and the indictment covers the period up until the 20th of June, 1999, we believe that this is irrelevant since this notice, even if it were indeed sent, was late. It was after the relevant period. The contents of the exhibit show that this report was published in the year 2000, and we would therefore like to move that this exhibit not be admitted into evidence because of its irrelevance. We would like to do that now. I believe that we have several problems with Exhibit P2228. This is a number of statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you help me just grasp a little more clearly what is your point of the irrelevance of the Exhibit P386? You've mentioned that it was written some time after the indictment period, but it's a report looking retrospectively at events, so it's not altogether clear to me what is the basis of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind all the materials that the Defence has gone through and the situation that was in place until this trial here today, and in light of the facts that I've presented already, to wit, that this material is not based on the direct knowledge of the witness, that he himself did not take part in the taking of the statements from the persons who are listed in this report - quite the opposite is the case, other people did that - and the Prosecution has been using this to prove that the Serbian authorities had been informed but in an irrelevant period because this was published after the period that is relevant for the indictment. Any such notice is completely irrelevant for the proceedings. It does not have any effect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- the witness is basing his views upon statements taken from persons by somebody other than the witness himself. I'm still not quite clear what it is you're saying about the date of the report. Why is the date determinative of its admissibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this exhibit has been used by the Prosecution to indicate that the Yugoslav authorities had been informed about the crimes being committed in Kosovo and Metohija in the relevant period and even before the relevant period in the course of 1998 and 1999. This witness took part in some research projects in 1998 and in 1999; however, this notice, or rather, the witness claims that his organisation sent those reports to the governments, including the Serbian government, through its web site, and this notice in this form was available only in the year 2000, after the war ended. It was sent to the Serbian government or the FRY government, and that is why I believe that any such notice actually came too late. It was post festum, so they failed to notify the authorities promptly. And of course after such reports were received, after the war ended, criminal proceedings were instituted in a number of cases. This was not done in the period relevant for the indictment. We have several pieces of evidence regarding this reporting. I think it is in 1998. And I will deal with them in the cross-examination naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Djurdjic. I believe I now see the point you are wanting to make. That is, that insofar as this report could be relied on by the Prosecution to prove knowledge by the Serbian governmental authorities. The report was not communicated to them until after the indictment period. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, Your Honour, I would like to say something about P2228. It is a compendium of statements taken under 92 bis from this witness, and these are statements from 1999 and -- yes, yes, Your Honour, 65 ter, P2228, they have only been tendered into evidence, so thank you for your correction. We have three statements here. First of all, those statements taken under 92 bis have not been admitted into evidence in the Milutinovic case in their entirety, only selected passages were admitted, in accordance with the objections that were raised. And this Defence would like to object to this exhibit for the following reasons: First of all, in e-court there is a page of the statement missing; it has been redacted, and it should be there. This probably happened due to a clerical error. We also have the following objections: The statements in the portions that have not been admitted so far are based on hearsay evidence on the one hand; and on the other hand, they contain inappropriate conclusions made by a fact witness, not an expert witness. This is in particular the case with the 1999 statement which contains summaries based on the statements of witnesses who were not eye-witnesses. Then we also have statements of persons that are summarised and we have no way of checking whether this person actually did say that. Here I'm talking about primarily about the statement of Mr. Bosko Drobnjak. And I think that those portions of the statements are inadmissible. In the portions that have not been admitted into evidence in the Milutinovic case, we have some inappropriate conclusions about -- which are inappropriate for a fact witness. He gives his testimony in a manner which would be appropriate for an expert witness who is an expert in history, and we believe that he should provide sources that he's basing his views on. This would in particular be the case if he were an expert witness. He has not done so, yet he has made certain conclusions. Furthermore, we believe that Witness Abrahams is not an impartial observer, and we believe that the reports that he himself drafted, inter alia, are based on selective data and that his reports and his evidence, his statements, could have been influenced by his relationship with the OTP of this Tribunal. It is quite obvious that the conclusions were not made on the basis of all the information available; and on the other hand, we don't know the sources that the historical conclusions are based on. And these are conclusions that only the Trial Chamber can actually present in the judgement, agreeing with them or disagreeing with them. But it is up to this Trial Chamber to make these kind of conclusions in the judgement at the end of the whole trial. And I would like to now highlight the most blatant parts of the statement, that pertains to the 1974 constitution and the assessments made by the witness about the political processes in the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s. Primarily, this witness was not a direct observer of these events, and he is not an expert witness. And had he been called here as an expert witness, he would have had to give us his sources for his expert conclusions. And now we have conclusions made by a fact witness, conclusions about the events that he did not participate in, and that is why we believe that those portions of his statements are inadmissible. Furthermore, the witness has not listed sources where his allegations or claims can be verified. Having studied the material, the Human Rights Watch had a comprehensive study, a historical study, that covered the period from 1990 to 1995 - that was their first report - so it was done at the time when the witness was not an official of that organisation at all. He did not take part in the research. And if he actually gave his statement on the basis of this report, we believe that this was not proper, and that is why we also think that those portions of his statement should not be admitted into evidence. And finally, the witness has made conclusions on the basis of rumours, unverified rumours, and facts and sources that are not quoted. So those are our reasons to object to the admission of the statements. Furthermore, the Defence moves that 65 ter Exhibit P438 not be admitted into evidence. I think that we're now going back to the problems that we had with the materials that were tendered through Mr. Neill Wright, and this Chamber has already ruled on that issue. This exhibit is a report of the Human Rights Watch organisation entitled: "Under Orders," and it is based on statements of persons who might -- and those statements can be qualified as hearsay. It is impossible to verify the claims, and it is unreliable evidence of the facts. On the other hand, the Defence is unable to cross-examine any of the witnesses that have provided the statements. And I would like to add, in none of the statements, unlike the statements that are taken in order to be used in the current proceedings, did -- were the witnesses warned that they should make their statements to the best of their knowledge and recollections. We -- I don't even know what the statements look like. Were they audio recorded? Were they handwritten? Were they typed up and then signed by the persons giving those statements, or was it done by the persons -- by the interviewer? We don't know what shape or form those statements are. And I would like to say, furthermore, that in this exhibit, even if we're talking only about the crime base - and there is also the management structure, the command and control, information from 1991, and the historical context - so even if we're talking only about the crime base, I believe that this is inadmissible primarily because those statements were taken in close collaboration with the Prosecution of this Tribunal in a selective manner, not on the basis of any random sampling. And the witness will explain to us how they actually selected the persons that they wanted to interview, how and why those statements were taken, to what end. But I believe that the reason that I have already put forward for my objection is a valid one. In particular, if we bear in mind that Mr. Abrahams has had contact with the OTP since 1998, since his stay in Albania. His first statement was given in March 1999 before the attack on the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was launched, I think it was the 15th or the 13th of March, that was the date of the first statement. And we will ascertain the ways in which the cooperation between the witness, his organisation on the one hand, and the Prosecution on the other hand, proceeded. But one thing is for sure: The witness ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that in 2000 and 2001 the witness was employed by the OTP of this Tribunal, he worked as an investigator; and in at least two cases, he worked as an investigator taking statements from witnesses. Unfortunately, one of the statements was admitted, I think, under 94 -- Rule 94, and we have yet to hear the evidence of another -- of the other witness. And this report contains completely inappropriate conclusions for a fact witness, and those conclusions pertain to the criminal responsibility of the accused, chain of command, and the structure in the FRY, the functioning of the MUP and the Yugoslav Army. So he is making conclusions that only the Trial Chamber is entitled to make in its judgement. Again, the sources for such conclusions are not reliable, in fact they're unknown, and some are based on interviews with some persons. We believe -- let me go back to the total of six statements made between February 1998 until the end of June 1999, all of the reports that pertain to that period are based on the statements of a total of 600 persons selected according to the criteria known only to the organisation that the witness worked for. He actually interviewed very few of those people in Albania and in Kosovo and Metohija. This is where he interviewed those alleged victims. We believe that, for aforementioned reasons, the Defence is entitled under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to move that this exhibit not be admitted into evidence. Let me just add as regards P2228 that -- or, in fact, there is no reason for me to do that now. If we'll have to do it, we'll do it at an appropriate time. Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me the time to present our objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will try my best to address all the long list of objections that have just been raised by my learned colleague. Starting by Exhibit 02228, which is the 92 bis package for this witness. I would -- which my learned colleague has objected, indicating that there are some inappropriate conclusions that pertain to an expert witness rather than a fact witness. This is, in fact, an inaccurate representation of the evidence that's in that statement, and this -- the conclusions and the observations that are made in the statement or the different statements by Mr. Abrahams are, in fact, based on his personal observation, his long history of work in the region, and his intensive interviews conducted with survivors and eye-witnesses to the events he describes. So I disagree with my colleague in that respect. It is accurate that some of the evidence or statements that Mr. Abrahams makes in his series of statements is based on hearsay evidence. Our position is that hearsay evidence is admissible, and it is for the Chamber to determine the weight it will attach to some of his conclusions in his statements that are based on hearsay evidence. I also want to correct my learned colleague with regard to the Neill Wright decision. He had indicated that we are in a situation similar to the Neill Wright decision. I want to remind Your Honours that Your Honours, in the Neill Wright decision with respect to attachment 4, did not find that attachment inadmissible because it contained portions of hearsay evidence; but the ruling of Your Honours was that the witness should be cross-examined on those portions and should provide evidence on how that information was obtained and how those reports were compiled. So the general statement made by my colleague is, first of all, not accurate; and we're in a different situation here where the witness will explain and already does so in his various statements the methodology used to obtain the information and will describe his work and research trips to the region. With regard to the allegations made with respect to his impartiality or lack thereof and his cooperation with the Office of the Prosecution in the past, we submit that this is a matter that is -- should be addressed in cross-examination. My learned colleague will have the opportunity to put that to Mr. Abrahams and -- during his cross-examination. As regards the statements that are made in his various statements with regard to the political background of the Kosovo conflict, again, it is our submission that this is -- these conclusions that are in his statements and these observations are based on his many years of work in the area and what he has been able to learn and observe during his time working in the region. So I would submit that Your Honours postpone the decision on this selection of statements, that is 02228, until after having heard the evidence of the witness and having allowed my learned colleague the opportunity to cross-examine on the issues that concern him. With regard to Exhibit 0386, this is a report on rape as a weapon of ethnic cleansing, my -- the submissions of my learned colleague are inaccurate in this respect. The witness indicates in his statement of July 2006 - and this is at paragraph 5, and this is Exhibit 65 ter 02227 - that he was involved in the -- in preparation of this report and conducted interviews that later were included in the -- in the report itself. And he was personally involved in the research for -- in the research of this report. My learned colleague raised the observation as to the notice if we were -- he's presuming we were tendering this for the purpose of notice and indicated that this report had been published or made published after the time-period of the indictment. We're, in fact, offering this report - and I again will ask Your Honours to postpone the decision of this report until after hearing the witness - but we're offering this report for the purpose of proving -- I'm sorry, I'm losing his voice -- for proving the general statements that are made within the report by the witness based on his interviews he conducted and what he was able to learn on the issue of sexual violence perpetrated against Kosovo Albanian women by forces of the FRY and Serbia. So I would again request Your Honours to postpone a decision of the admissibility of this exhibit until after having heard the testimony of the witness on this issue. Now, with regard to "Under Orders" which is 65 ter 00438, my learned colleague has made some lengthy objections with regard to this exhibit. I would like to point out at the outset that we are not intending to tender the entire report. We have prepared extracts of the report which have been uploaded under Exhibit 65 ter 00438.01, and we have notified the Defence of this. We are only intending to tender the portions of the report which the witness not only personally drafted but he also was himself involved in researching and in conducting interviews with survivors and eye-witnesses. So although these portions of the report do contain hearsay, again it is our position that this is first-hand hearsay, these portions of the report are relevant to the charges of the indictment, they corroborate evidence that has been heard or will be heard with respect to our crime base, and referred or contain the witness's personal observations during his research trips to Kosovo. So those are my submissions. I may have forgotten one or two points, and if Your Honours need me to state a position on another point raised by my learned colleague that I may have omitted, I'm happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Should the Chamber decide to postpone its decision until after the testimony of the witness, we are prepared to provide our arguments in writing should the Chamber believe that to be useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that it would not be able to do -- give proper consideration to all the matters raised in Mr. Djurdjic's lengthy and careful submission in an extempore decision today. The practical course in the Chamber's view will be to hear the evidence offered but to decide later, in view of its consideration of the objections raised and the response made by Ms. Kravetz, what parts, if any, will be admitted of the evidence to which objection is made. If it becomes our view that some parts or all parts that are subject of objection should not be received, of course we would put that evidence aside and it would not form part of the basis of our deliberation. So on that basis then, the objection being noted and being in due course the subject of our decision, we will proceed to hear the evidence that is offered in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would like to add that if it was the wish of Your Honours, we are also happy to make written submissions in this respect with regard to the different exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're grateful for that and Mr. Djurdjic's offer, Ms. Kravetz, but we think we've had pretty detailed submissions, and we don't see that we need to trouble you to go through the process of putting it all down again in writing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We apologise for having kept you. There was some significant issues raised which we needed to deal with. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Frederick Cronig Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In New York City, US, November 2, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I am a senior researcher with the organisation Human Rights Watch, although currently on a six-month leave as of May 1st.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And very briefly, what is Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch is a non-governmental organisation that documents and publicises human rights violations around the world. We accept no government funds, and we do research in more than 70 countries without regard for any political orientation or in support or against of any religious, ethnic, or other group. And my work in particular is now documenting violations in crisis areas and particularly armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, since we're both speaking the same language today, I'm going to ask you just to pause between question and answer so your answers can be recorded appropriately by the court reporter today. Since when have you been employed by Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I began my full-time employment in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during your time with Human Rights Watch, have you had the opportunity to cover events in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, extensively.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And have you specifically had the opportunity to work on -- and cover events in the province of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, also extensively.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Since when has your work been focused on events in the former Yugoslavia, specifically on Kosovo province, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, my first work in the Balkan region was in Albania in 19 -- from 1995 to 1997. I first visited Kosovo in the summer of 1995, but my first human rights investigations there were in 1996, summer, I believe July. And from that time until 2000, I undertook multiple missions - I would have to count to be precise - but approximately ten, to document violations of human rights and also violations of international humanitarian law by all parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in relation to your work with Human Rights Watch in Kosovo, did you provide several statements to the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal, one dated March 1999, a second dated January 2002, and a third one dated May 2002?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have the opportunity to review these statements?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having had the opportunity to review the statements, are you satisfied that the information contained in these statements is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note you're deferring the decision on the tendering of Exhibit 02228, but I wish to submit it to Your Honours for admission at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be assigned P00738 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, did you provide a further statement to the Office of the Prosecution in July 2006?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I did. I don't remember the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the information contained in the statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter 02227, and I seek to tender that into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00739 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe my learned colleague's objections - and I may be wrong here - concerned only the first exhibit but not 0227 -- 02227. So I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there objection to the document 65 ter P2227, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. My learned friend, Ms. Kravetz, is fully right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00739, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, did you also testify previously in this Tribunal in the case of Milutinovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, have you had the chance to read over the transcript of your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today as you were asked during that previous court testimony, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: To the best of my ability, yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter 05187, and I seek to tender that into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't believe this is subject to objection, in which event, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00740, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, before turning to your work for Human Rights Watch in Kosovo, I would like to ask you some general questions about the work of the organisation in the region. In your statement - and this is at page 10 of 02228, which has been marked for identification - you indicate that Human Rights Watch began reporting about human rights violations in Kosovo in 1990. And you say that between 1990 and October 2001 there were approximately 16 reports published by Human Rights Watch in addition to over a hundred briefing reports, press release, and advocacy papers. Could you explain to the Court the methodology used by Human Rights Watch in documenting human rights violations in this region.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, the -- the fundamental methodology which applies to this region, I mean Kosovo, the Balkans, and every country where we work, is to conduct field investigations. So researchers like myself who are trained in conducting these types of investigations conduct what we call missions, which means going to the country or region in question and interviewing the witnesses or victims of human rights or IHL, humanitarian law, violations. We also try to get information and, if possible, interview perpetrators. We visit the scenes of the alleged violations. We collect corroborative material or material that -- that will shed light on the -- the allegations, whether it's to prove it or disprove it, such as court records, medical reports, autopsy reports. And then also secondary sources, when they can shed lights on angles or perspectives. So we would never rely on secondary sources solely, but we would use them to tell a fuller picture of a case in question. So it's these field research missions that form the crux of our methodology.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how do you document or record the information that is collected during these field missions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Most usually it is written, in written form, notes. Increasingly -- on occasion and increasingly with the digital age, my colleagues have recorded interviews; but usually when recordings are taken then written notes are also taken in case there is a battery -- a malfunction or a battery dies. And these notes form the -- the essence of our reports. We go back and use them. In a way, they're witness statements and -- we call them -- in Human Rights Watch we call them testimony. And it's very important, whenever possible, we conduct these interviews in a one-on-one setting, so we identify the witness or the victim or the person who has information, and we try to speak with them in private. We are trained not to use leading questions, but the interviews are more in the form of open narrative so individuals can tell us information that they wish. And of course we ask questions to focus them but to avoid leading questions. And lastly, we seek to get complete pictures so we would never publish a report or make an accusation based on one witness. We would require multiple witnesses whose statements were corroborative, and that means sometimes going into great detail, so these interviews can take a long time, they can be many hours and sometimes multiple visits to get very precise specifics that can be checked and help us determine the veracity of the person's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken about the reports that are prepared by Human Rights Watch when these field research missions are conducted. I'm interested in the reports that were prepared with regard to events in Kosovo and would like to know if you could explain a little the procedure followed by Human Rights Watch to disseminate reports that it produces after conducting these sort of investigations.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Our reports are widely disseminated to a variety of institutions and individuals and organisations. They go to the media, this is a very important recipient of our work; they go to international organisations, both non-governmental organisations and international organisations like the United Nations; and they go to governments, they go widely to governments that are following the issue about which the report is -- about the violations that the report is documenting, but also to the government that -- that is implicated in these violations or that we're accusing is -- the officials from that government have committed these violations. And the same goes for armed groups because we research in particular -- in areas of conflict, we -- you have international conflicts, where we'll look at both -- two or more governments that are involved or the armed forces of those governments, but we will also examine armed groups. In the Kosovo case, the Kosovo Liberation Army is the example, but all over the world we'll look at these armed groups as well and try our best to disseminate, make sure that they get our reports and our statements. Usually the reports are disseminated through multiple means. There's the printed version, whereby the physical reports are sent via post. During the time in question, that was done. It's done much less today because of the prevalence of the internet, but back then it was done on a standard basis. We also distributed our press releases by fax, and every report would have a press release announcing the report; and also by e-mail. And by 1996 -- I think by 1996 we had instituted a distribution system by e-mail so that every statement and every report was distributed in that -- in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we're concentrating specifically on Kosovo, you spoke about dissemination of reports to governments you thought were implicated in the human rights violations you had documented. In the case of Kosovo, if you are looking at violations that you believe were committed by entities that belonged to either the Serbian or Yugoslav government, would these reports have been sent to authorities in those governments or institutions within those governments?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, they would. I can only speak to the period in which I was working on these issues, which was from 1995 and with Kosovo from 1996, and we did undertake efforts to make sure that all of our statements and reports -- anything we produced publicly was distributed to the relevant officials on the Serbian and the Yugoslav level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about dissemination via e-mail. How was this carried out with respect to Yugoslav and Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We maintained a list, a distribution list, for each country in which we worked, and at that time, you know, that included all the countries of the Balkans and specifically the Yugoslav list was -- was maintained so that everyone on that list would receive our -- receive our product.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And -- so was this list regularly updated? I mean, if a person changed position and a new person was appointed, would that be -- would your mailing list be updated to reflect those changes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, they would. The list was constantly being refined, updated, and adapted as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And with respect to Serbian authorities, did this list include representatives of the Ministry of Interior, the Serbian Ministry of Interior, MUP?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The Serbian Ministry of Interior as well as the Yugoslav Ministry of Interior were on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall which other entities of the Serbian government would have been included in your mailing list?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army was on our list, the Presidencies, I believe, Serbian and Yugoslav Presidencies were on it -- the list -- at least some of the lists because the mailing lists and the e-mail lists might not always have been exactly the same. The Ministries of Justice on the republican and federal level. That's it, interior, justice, the army, and the Presidencies, if -- to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to turn to your work in Kosovo during 1998. Did you -- you have spoken about different research missions that you conducted in the region. Did you conduct any research missions to Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When was the first mission that you conducted to the -- to Kosovo on that year?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The first mission was in May of 1998, I believe it extended into June, about three weeks long, May/June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that mission?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: At that point, hostilities had erupted, had begun, between Serbian and Yugoslav forces on one side and KLA on the other side. There had been a series of violent incidents involving -- in which civilians had been killed and increasing reports of serious violations of both human rights and international humanitarian law. So we wanted to investigate those allegations, and to do so required going into the field, as we call it, to conduct this research.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you conduct your research in any specific area of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we ended up focusing on a couple of areas but a primary focus was on the region of central Kosovo that's known as Drenica. It encompasses two municipalities, I believe it's Glogovac and Srbica municipalities. This was one of the areas which -- in which the KLA was very active. Some people call it the cradle of the KLA where it began, and there had been some very violent incidents there in which large numbers of civilians were killed in at least three villages that I'm aware of. So we went there to investigate the circumstances around those civilian deaths. That was the primary focus. I believe I also spent time in the other area that was heavily affected, which is the western areas of Kosovo, particularly between Pec and Djakovica, the area of Decan, there was also a lot of fighting in that area and allegations of serious violations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were three villages where there had been civilian death and that you had investigated. Do you recall the names of those villages?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, in Drenica the three most prominent cases were Prekaz, Likosane, and Cirez. There were different -- Likosane and Cirez are neighbouring villages and that might be considered one incident. I believe it was March 20 -- February 28/March 1, and I believe 20 people we considered to be civilians were killed in those two villages, including ten members of one family that we believed were -- were executed, members of the Ahmeti family, based on eye-witnesses who told us what happened. And in Prekaz was another story. There were two incidents in Prekaz, one in January and one in March -- I think it was March 5th. And the March 5th incident was the most serious. There was increasingly well-known KLA member named Adem Jashari who had had numerous altercations with the police; he was definitely engaged in militant activity and the security forces surrounded his compound, besieged it, and there were in the end I believe it's 58 members of his family were killed. I believe Jashari and some of his family members were also fighting back, but in the end 58 members of his family died except -- there was one survivor, one 11-year-old girl named Besarta. But I did not conduct in-depth investigations into the Prekaz incident. I focused more on Likosane and Cirez. And in that case we determined that there had been some KLA attacks and some policemen had been killed, and then the response led to the high number of civilian deaths, I believe it was more than 25. I remember four brothers of one family and a pregnant woman I remember in particular Rukija Nebija who were killed in those attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during this research mission, were you working alone or were other colleagues of Human Rights Watch working with you during this investigation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: On that mission, on that investigation, I worked alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you prepare a report in -- with regard to your findings during this investigation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of that report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It's called "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo," and it's based on that research mission and directly after I travelled to northern Albania, because in the western area there were at least 10.000 ethnic Albanians who had fled Kosovo into -- across the mountains into Albania, so I interviewed them in northern Albania and that also formed a substantial basis for our conclusions in that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you solely involved in the drafting of this report or did other persons at Human Rights Watch collaborate in the drafting of this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I was the sole drafter, but all of our reports, this one as well as every other, go through a rigorous review process. They're reviewed first within the geographic division, in this case it's the Europe and Central Asia division; they're reviewed by our programme office; and they're reviewed by our legal office. So this report, like all others, went through that process.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when this report was made public by Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't exactly. It would have been probably the end of 1998 if I'm not mistaken, latter month, October 1998 perhaps. I'm sorry I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we had spoken earlier about the dissemination of reports. Would this report have been disseminated according to the general procedure of Human Rights Watch, that is, via mailing list to the different authorities and to the media?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, this report would have been disseminated in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this report is Exhibit 00437, and I seek to tender it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00741, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. Abrahams, when preparing this report, did you try to obtain information from the Serbian authorities as to what had occurred in the Drenica region?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How did you try to obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: During the mission, I requested and received a meeting with a Serbian official in Pristina, Kosovo capital. He was the local representative of the Ministry of Information by the name of Bosko Drobnjak. And I had a discussion with Mr. Drobnjak in which I presented some of our concerns. I gave him a list of ethnic Albanians who had gone missing, I believe that had at least 12 names on it. He replied by saying this was the government's legitimate fight against what he called terrorism, and it was not within his competency to give me an answer about the missing persons as well as some of the other questions I had about the behaviour of the Serbian and Yugoslav security forces. So when I returned to New York, I prepared a series of letters which we sent from New York via fax to the relevant authorities in Serbia and Yugoslavia in which we asked questions and solicited their response to the various allegations we had heard in Kosovo -- I had heard during the research mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to have Exhibit 65 ter 00542 brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This document will appear on the screen before you, Mr. Abrahams. I don't know if you have the document. There.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like just for the English to be displayed for the witness, please. Just the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you explain what it is, this document.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is the letter that I referenced earlier, namely, our questions to Minister Stojiljkovic, the Minister of Interior of the Republic of Serbia. These are the questions that I sent after the research mission in May and June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm unfortunately having a problem with my e-court system. It seems to be crashing quite frequently, but we'll try to continue like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told that all systems are presently disabled in all courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Well, glad to know it's not just me. So if we could scroll down this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see that this letter was sent by Ms. Holly Cartner. Could you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Holly Cartner was and still is the director of the Europe and Central Asia division, at Human Rights Watch, my boss at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now did you receive any response to this letter sent to Mr. Stojiljkovic in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I notice that in the letter you are asking about information on policemen who may have died, and you're also asking about information about abuses committed by government authorities, and you indicate in the last question: "Have any policemen been disciplined or criminally charged for exceeding the legal limits while performing their duties in Kosovo ..." Was it usually the case that when conducting your investigation you tried to investigate violations committed by all sides in a conflict?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: More than just tried. That was explicitly our mandate, to investigate violations by all parties to the conflict, not just in the Kosovo case but in every armed conflict that we -- in which we work; and now I've worked in many. So we were definitely interested to know about attacks on members of the police as well as the army and to hear about allegations of violations committed by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to understand, was it the general practice of Human Rights Watch to try to obtain the position of the authorities you thought were -- might be implicated in the abuses that you were observing on the ground, or is this an exceptional case that you were sending letters to government authorities in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No, we endeavoured to obtain the views of the government side or of the forces we were -- we believed might have committed these violations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would that have been the case for each one of the research missions that you conducted in Kosovo during the time that you were working there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: To the best of our ability, we made these requests, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please have -- oh, I would seek to tender this exhibit into evidence before we move to the next one. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00742, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now please have 65 ter 00544 up on the screen. And if we could display the second page of that exhibit only in the English for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a version of the same letter that we submitted after my mission to the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: With the different letters that you sent out when you were conducting this research contain essentially the same questions or did you change or modify the requests for information depending on the entity you were addressing these letters?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We modified the questions depending on the entity; in this case, to specifically ask about incidents or information involving the VJ, the Vojska Jugoslavije.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this would have been a letter that was sent within the context of the same research that we have been talking about conducted with respect to the Drenica region?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this exhibit at this stage. This is 65 ter 00544.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00743, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are a series of these letters, there are seven in total, which are referred to in the exhibit that I have already tendered, the 65 ter 2227, and they are described or explained at pages 2 to 3 of these exhibits. I'm not -- I do not wish to go -- show the witness each one of these letters, but as they are contained within that statement that has already been admitted by Your Honours, I would seek to tender the whole -- the remaining five letters which are described in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The five will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I will call out each one of the 65 ter numbers so they get assigned an exhibit number. The first one is 00540.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00744, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00745.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00746.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00747.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the last one is 00546.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00748.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to be moving to a different topic now. I think -- I don't know if this is an appropriate moment for the break. I know we're five minutes early --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps that will be a convenient time. We will adjourn for the half-hour and resume at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, before the break we were talking about your research missions to Kosovo in 1998, and I would like now to ask you some questions about a report that you referred to in your statement of July 2006 and also in your previous statements, and this is at paragraph 19 of P739. And this is a report called "A Week of Terror in Drenica" which you say you co-authored with a colleague. Could you tell us what this report was about?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I returned to Kosovo in September 1998, and during that time the Serbian and Yugoslav forces were on a military offensive to rout the KLA from territory that the Albanian fighters had -- had taken control of. And we heard of an incident - I believe I learned of it on September 28th - an incident in the Drenica region in which a large number of people from one family had reportedly been killed, civilians. So my colleague and I travelled to this village. The offensive -- the government offensive had stopped at that time. I believe it stopped on the 26th of September. And we succeeded to reach the village. It was a place called Obrinje, Gornje Obrinje to be precise. And when we arrived there, we witnessed the villagers taking from a wooded area the bodies of civilians who had been killed. There were -- when we arrived they were carrying out three individuals, all of them children, on a kind of makeshift stretcher and there were other bodies in a wooded area just outside the village. I believe it was seven bodies of women and children in total. And they were burying them in a nearby field. 14 members of that family, it's the Delijaj family were killed, and we saw the bodies of the seven plus the three they were taking out. So we began an investigation that day which lasted for about three weeks. We ended up returning -- my colleague and I left Kosovo and then returned again in November to complete the investigation. And our findings were produced in this -- in this report that you mentioned "A week of terror in Drenica."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You spoke about a colleague of yours who was involved in this investigation. Can you please indicate what was his name or her name?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Peter Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you learned of this incident in the village on September 28th, do you recall -- yes, before I move to my question could you please spell out the last name of your colleague.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: B-o-u-c-k-a-e-r-t.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you said that you had learned of this incident on September 28th. Do you recall from whom you had -- you learned about it, you initially heard about this incident?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I initially heard about it from some -- from an ethnic Albanian friend who was a journalist in Pristina, worked for the newspaper "Koha Ditore," and he didn't know the details but told me that something had happened in this village of Gornje Obrinje. So based on that information, we decided to take a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that your research lasted for about three weeks. Could you briefly explain the methodology that you used during this research that you conducted into this incident.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, in this case, we were ourselves ocular witnesses, not to the killing itself, in that sense no; but we saw the bodies as they lay there. And that formed on important part of our results because the wounds were consistent with the testimony we collected, and I can go into detail about what we saw on the bodies if you -- if that's helpful. But the investigation then involved the in-depth interviews with the people we believed had information about the incident. That means the family members of those affected plus others who lived in the village of Obrinje and in the general area. There was another incident in the nearby village of Golubovac where 14 men were executed. That also was part of that report. So we interviewed a large number. I would have to look at the report to tell you exactly how many people we interviewed. All of the interviews are in -- are footnoted, the name if appropriate -- I mean if the person doesn't request anonymity, the date and place of the interview, and also my notes to tell you how many people. But we interviewed definitely more than two dozen people, for sure more than two dozen, who had some information about this incident. We also looked at official statements from the Serbian and Yugoslav government. In this case there had been fighting in the village of Obrinje between the KLA and Serbian forces. There had been fighting in the Drenica area in general. And some Serbian policemen had been killed. And their names were made public by the government. So we included those details, the fact that there are had been fighting in the area is very relevant to trying -- to determining whether there had been a violation or not. And all of that taken together was -- was used to help us reach our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that you interviewed about two dozen people who could provide information of this incident. Did you interview each person separately?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I would have to refer to my notes to tell you whether each and every individual was interviewed in a one-on-one setting, but by all means that is our aim. We strive to do that at every time and it is for the most part possible. We make -- we take great efforts to ensure that atmosphere, but there are times when it's not possible. And so I can't testify that every single interview was in that setting, but the vast and overwhelming majority of them definitely were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did these persons that you interviewed in Gornje Obrinje tell you about what had happened there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: They testified that -- that there had been fighting in the area and that the KLA had been -- had established a base in the nearby village called Likovac, but the Serbian forces perhaps with -- also with participation of the Yugoslav Army had surrounded the area. There was shelling of the area. And civilians, mostly women and children, had fled the village of Obrinje and tried to take shelter in a forested area, maybe a kilometre away from the village. And that's the -- that's the area where we found the bodies later. Other members of the family and villagers, not just the Delijaj family, fled in other directions. Some of them tried to hide in the village itself and a few of those people were found killed. Mostly those were older members of the family who were -- apparently they were too old to flee on foot. And then they testified about returning on the 28th, I think, if not the 27th, returning to the area and finding the bodies of their relatives in this -- in this wooded area and in other parts of the village. There was -- in one case there was an eye-witness to killings. It happened, I believe, I would have to -- the Hysenaj family, it was a woman from the Hysenaj family within another part of the Obrinje village. She witnessed what she said were the police interrogating and she claimed killing three older residents who had stayed behind. This was also in the Obrinje village but not members of the Delijaj family, another family. I would have to check the report to give you the names of those victims, but it's recorded. And that corroborated what we found, I should add. When we entered the village on the 29th, we saw those bodies, three bodies, it was, I believe, two elderly men and an elderly woman, and we saw their bodies lying there and -- but then proceeded on to the Delijaj family, which were the bodies we found in the forest. And then in the subsequent interviews, we learned how those three people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And with respect to these bodies that you were able to observe yourself, what sort of wounds were you able to observe on the bodies, if any?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I took the closest look at the seven bodies that were in a kind of gully, and it was a dry -- sort of a dry stream bed. They were -- I believe it was two children and five adults, and most of them, not all, but most had wounds to the head. One of them had been pregnant. That I was -- that I didn't recognise myself. I was told that by the victim's husband. And some of them showed signs of mutilation. What was -- looked to me like possible knife wounds. One man who was not in the gully, he was a little bit towards -- on the path, more towards -- towards the village, he was an elderly gentleman who was named Piazit [phoen] Delijaj, his throat had been slit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to also having had access to official statements of Yugoslav and Serbian authorities. Can you explain what sort of entity had issued those statements and what was contained in those statements that you had access to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Regarding this incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, regarding this incident, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the statements were released by what was called the media centre - I think it was called the Serbian media centre, but maybe it was just called the media centre - which had been established in Pristina with a base at the Hotel Grand, which was the main hotel in Pristina, and it was never officially linked to the state, to the government; but it was everyone's understanding that it was a government-run or in the very least government-supported press centre. And they released statements regularly about attacks on police and army, and in this case they did the same, releasing at least one statement with the names of some of the policemen. I believe some of them were reservists and others were regular police who had been killed in and around Obrinje in the fighting that preceded the incident to which I referred.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, did you or your colleague take photographs at the location that you visited, at Gornje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 00642 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise the photograph that is before you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is depicted there.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: These are two children from the Delijaj family being taken from this forested area to the nearby open field for burial. I think I mentioned a makeshift stretcher and that would be this basically two pieces of wood with a fabric in between. This photograph was taken by my colleague, Peter Bouckaert, while I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this photograph, it's 65 ter 00642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be -- they will be received. One photograph, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00749, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now move to 65 ter 00653, if that could be displayed for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you please comment on the photograph that's put up on the screen before you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is one of the Delijaj family members, a woman, as we found her in this so-called gully in -- outside the village of Obrinje, taken by my colleague, Peter Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this would have been, again, a photograph taken during the course of the same visit to Gornje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. These are one of the seven bodies that we saw, that I saw, in the gully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit, 00653.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00750, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now see 00679, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is one of the Delijaj children as we found him in the gully outside of Obrinje on September 29th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Peter Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have spoken about having seen seven bodies. Do you recall how many of those bodies were bodies of women or children?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely. I believe two of the bodies were children and five were women, but my recollection is a little hazy after all of these years. It is presented in the report, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could -- I seek to tender that before I move to the next photograph, this is 00679.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00751, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now move to 00702, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is depicted on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This photograph was taken in a village called Plocica, which is in the Drenica region just a few kilometres north of the Pristina-Pec road. We entered the village on September 26th and just after the Serbian and Yugoslav offensive had stopped. We actually observed a large convoy of military vehicles leaving the region -- leaving this area. And when we entered Plocica, the villagers were just returning. They had been hiding in the forest. And we asked them what happened. And in interviews they told us that their area had been -- had come under attack from shelling and that police forces had entered the village so they fled into the nearby forest. And when they returned they found their village in this condition. The village had been heavily destroyed, and it appeared to us as if it had been -- large sections of the civilian infrastructure had been purposely set on fire. I say that because the homes -- this photograph is a good example. The homes were burning - this was still on fire - from the inside. The walls were still standing. There were no burn marks on the exterior walls, but the inside of the structures were burning. I recall seeing at least three haystacks that had been individually burned, which suggested to me that they had been set on fire. There was a long briar fence that had been burned, and I also found at least one benzine bottle of -- I mean, a plastic bottle that smelled of benzine. I also recall finding in a field near to this home a box of empty ammunition and probably a mortar -- probably mortars -- a box that held mortars. This particular -- this particular structure was a food warehouse, and inside the house were melons and sacks of flour that were on fire. I believe this gentleman is the owner of the house. I'm not sure exactly who he is, but this was taken by a man named Wade Goddard who was a photographer for the New York Times; he was travelling with us. I should add one additional recollection were the farm animals. I remember seeing three burned sheep in the village and also a cow and the cow had been shot, had been shot in the head, which was -- after that I subsequently in the region saw many cows, at least ten cows that had been also killed in this way but not in Plocica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you -- were you able to observe any evidence that there had been fighting in Plocica before you -- your team arrived?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No. We were not able -- did not see any evidence of hostilities. By that I mean we found no bullet casings. The only weaponry we found was the box of mortar fire, which incidentally I should say had Cyrillic writing on the outside of the box. So we took it to mean it was Yugoslav Army equipment, perhaps police. But we didn't find any bullet casings. We didn't find any marks on the structures that would indicate fighting, such as impact marks of bullets or other forms of ammunition. And we found no signs of defensive positions or other, let's say, physical signs of the KLA's presence, bunkers or berms or anything that they might have prepared, which we did see in other villages where the KLA had been fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that my learned colleague is on his fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it appears to me that now we have gone beyond testifying about facts. We have now gone into conclusions that would more properly be reached by a military expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The only evidence so far is that there were no signs of presence of fighters, bunkers, or berms, which is a military emplacement. That seems to be within the competence of the observation of any person, Mr. Djurdjic. So carry on, please, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, is the damage we see here on the photograph and what you have described as a barn consistent with the damage that you were able to observe on other civilian property in the village of Plocica?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it's wholly consistent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this photograph into evidence it's 65 ter 00702.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00752, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we were talking about your investigation into the incident in the killing in the village of Gornje Obrinje and the report that you and your colleague drafted. Do you recall when that report was made public, "A Week of Terror in Drenica"?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I believe it was February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And again, we had been speaking earlier about dissemination of reports. Would this report have also been sent to both Serbian and Yugoslav authorities in accordance with your usual procedure?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it would have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know if it was also disseminated to the press, if it was sent -- copies were sent to the press at the time when it was released?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Definitely, and I should add that this incident also received widespread international media attention. I mentioned the photographer from the New York Times. We were also accompanied, we were travelling with, a journalist from the New York Times, Jane Perlez, and she wrote a front-page article in the New York Times about this very incident with photographs of the victims. So this -- this Gornje Obrinje case received widespread coverage, as did our subsequent report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when this article would have been published in the New York Times? I mean, was this when you were still investigating or after you had concluded your three-week mission in the region?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No, the article would have been published just days after the journalist and photographer had visited the scene, so the -- I don't know the precise date, but it would have been September 30th, maybe the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the report into evidence this is 65 ter 00441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00753, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I would like now -- I would like to move to your work in Kosovo in 1999. Did you return to Kosovo in early 1999 to conduct an additional investigative research mission in the region?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I visited Kosovo four times in 1998 to conduct research, and then again in February of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of your visit -- your mission to Kosovo in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It was to continue our investigations about IHL violations, international humanitarian law, and in particular the focus of my research was to be the alleged destruction of civilian property in -- in parts of Kosovo. We began that research, but because the NATO bombardment of Yugoslavia began on March 24th, we never concluded the research and never published a report with our findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And on that occasion, were you on your own conducting this investigation or were you with other colleagues from Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In February I was with a colleague, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you take any photographs of what you were able to observe during this February mission?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall if you were specifically in any area of the province? I mean, was your research focused on any specific area of the province or did you tour different municipalities?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We toured extensively, but I recall focusing on the western area, particularly around the city of Pec, and also in and around Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why did you decide to focus on that area in western Kosovo and Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In that area we had been receiving the most consistent and credible allegations of serious violations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And serious violations by whom, by which of the parties to the fighting?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: By both -- by both of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
