utterances.text: And from whom had you been receiving these allegations?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: From a long list of sources. They were coming from other human rights organisations, both local and international, they were coming from the media, they were coming from local authorities, they were coming from the network of individuals in Kosovo that I had developed, people we trusted to tell us about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 00700 up on the screen and I would like to have page 5 displayed for the witness. Yes, this is the 65 ter -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise the image that's -- the photograph that's up on the screen, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this is a photo of the village called Lodja just outside of Pec.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who took this photograph, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would this have been a photograph taken during this mission that you were describing in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain any information as to what had happened there? We see houses without roofs and that have been burnt?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, I first visited Lodja in September of 1998 -- or better said, I tried to visit Lodja. At that time, it was occupied by the Serbian police. We saw them in uniform, and they denied us access to the village. I should say that even prior to that the KLA had definitely been in the village, I believe in July; but when I arrived in September, the police were there. They didn't let us in. This -- when I returned then in February of 1999 and took this photograph, they had left. We were able to enter the village. And that's when we observed and photographed the destruction that's depicted here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7 of this same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is depicted there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: These are private homes, typical Albanian homes, just outside of Suva Reka. I don't recall the exact name of the district, but within a few kilometres of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would this have also been a photograph taken during your same February mission that you have been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain information as to who had burned these homes, what had happened in this area?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Witnesses claimed that Serbian forces had burned these homes. I don't, at this point, recall the details of those incidents. What was clear to me is that they had been burned from inside. Again, the lack of -- the absence of the roof -- the wooden roofs that had been burned and very limited scarring, burn marks, on the exterior, only when the fire appeared to have come out from a window.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could look at page 8 of this same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I do, but I'm afraid I'm not certain where -- what village it was taken. I believe in the Drenica area, probably Obrinje, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you explain what is depicted here on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It was -- it's a destroyed mosque, that's for sure, and I remember seeing a number of these in the Drenica area, but I don't recall the precise village. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine. And would this have also been a photograph taken by you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could look at page 10 of this same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Abrahams, if you could explain what is depicted on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: These -- this is also a mosque with substantial destruction to the roof and minaret, again in the Drenica region. I could easily figure out which village by looking back at my reports and notes, but sitting here I'm not certain which village it was taken in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain any information while you were there as to how this mosque had been damaged and by whom?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Local residents told us that it had been damaged by Serbian forces, but I do not recall the specifics of that allegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, page 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would this be a photograph of the same mosque we saw earlier?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, it's the same mosque as the previous photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence. There are additional photographs to this exhibit that I have not shown to the witness. The exhibit is 65 ter 00700. The photographs I have not shown to the witness are described or explained in his statement, these are page 12 and 13 of the statement of May 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand you seek to tender five photographs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, the photographs that I have shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Photographs under page 5, 7, 8, and 10, Your Honours, and 11 will be assigned P00754.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I now want to move to the period of the NATO bombing. Could you please tell us how Human Rights Watch coordinated the coverage of the NATO bombing in 1999.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: When the bombing began, we mobilised a team of researchers to the border areas with Kosovo. The international media and monitors from the OSCE were leaving, either on their own or being expelled, Kosovo. So entering the province was not an option for us, either legally, meaning we wouldn't be allowed in, and also for our security. So we sent researchers to the area of northern Albania and Macedonia where they were interviewing ethnic Albanian refugees who were leaving and, as they told us, being expelled from Kosovo. I stayed in New York for the initial period to coordinate the project. We sent our first researcher to north Albania within a few days, I believe it was three days after the start of the bombing so that would be around March 27th or 8th, and we had a researcher present in both cases for the full extent of the NATO campaign, which I believe lasted 78 days. I myself went in April to northern Albania, spent a few weeks up there interviewing the refugees coming into the area of Kukes, the town, and in the north; and then I went to Macedonia to do the same. In both places, large refugee camps had been established. So we interviewed refugees as they came across the border immediately and also then in the camps where they were being sheltered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about interviewing refugees as they were crossing the border into northern Albania, into Kukes. Do you recall what they were saying or what reasons they were giving for having left their homes and crossed over into northern Albania based on the interviews you conducted and what you were able to hear from these persons?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The interview subjects uniformly told us that they had left their homes because they had been forcibly expelled by security forces from either Serbia or Yugoslavia, meaning the army. Some of them left out of fear of expulsion, in other words, maybe they were not directly forced out of their villages but all the neighbouring villages had been and they got the message and left before they themselves were evicted. In many cases, these interviewees talked of killings in their home villages that typically -- a typical example would be that the area was surrounded and security forces separated the men from the women. The women were told to leave the area and sent to the border district where they had to cross out of Kosovo, and the men were kept behind, searched, interrogated. But in a disturbing number of cases, in villages that I could mention and which we reported, these men were -- were executed and there are some specific examples where that took place. Along the way, a lot of these people told us that they were harassed and robbed. Actually, theft and looting was more the exception than the norm that people had their wedding rings taken, their money, and other valuables by police, army, and also paramilitary units that were operating at that time. They also spoke about something we called identity cleansing, which is that along the way, and especially on the border, they were stripped of their identity documents. Sometimes cars had their licence plates removed, and people were forced to enter into Albania or Macedonia without any personal documentation. We interpreted this as a -- as an attempt to limit or restrict or prevent -- prevent their return to Kosovo. But I won't speculate on the motivation but simply the fact that many people said their documents had been taken by state security forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, were these persons that you were interviewing as they were crossing the border into Kukes, were they coming from area particular area of Kosovo or were they coming from different municipalities across the province?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: They came from a wide geographic area, but predominantly they came from the western areas of Kosovo, this would be anywhere from Djakovica, north to Pec, even north-west of that -- actually north-east of that, Istok area, Suva Reka area. In general, the people who went south to Macedonia were from the eastern parts of Kosovo, from Pristina, Lipljan, Vucitrn, and those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about cases where the interviewees would tell you about killings that happened in their villages and you said that there was some specific examples that came to mind. Now, could you -- do you recall any of those examples that you heard while you were conducting these interviews at the border?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. One of the very serious cases I recall is -- happened in the village of Bela Crkva, where the men were separated from the women and children and held in a kind of stream bed, where forces opened fire on them. We interviewed multiple witnesses, not just to the shooting but also to the incident as a whole, in other words, woman who said they had been separated from their men plus the men who had -- had been present, and we interviewed some survivors. In Bela Crkva I remember very vividly one survivor who testified about bodies falling on top of him, and he himself had been hit by a bullet. We took him to see a doctor and indeed he had a bullet, if I remember correctly, it was lodged in his shoulder. And 30-some odd people died in Bela Crkva. I remember quite well the testimony we got from villagers from a place called Meja. In that village they said that possibly up to 300 people had been -- had been killed, and that was a very interesting case because -- if you want I can go -- I don't know if details are of service to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, you can briefly explain, yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Okay. The Meja case was interesting because we first heard news of it in the morning as women crossed into Albania without their men, and we asked, Well, why are you coming alone, just women and children. And they said, We come from this area around Meja, and they separated us from our husbands and sons and fathers. Then in the middle of the day, I believe this was April 27th, in the middle of the day I interviewed women, refugees who said, We came through that same route, through Meja, and we saw men, we witnessed men kneeling by the side of the road in the detention of the police. And then we interviewed women who came through in the end of the day, April 27th, who said, We saw an even larger number of people and there were at least two witnesses who said they saw dead bodies who had been -- were literally piled up and on the side of the road. And they estimated that it was 300 bodies. And I specifically remember asking how they could do that because when you're afraid are you going to count bodies and if they're tumbled on top of each other. And I remember them describing that they were -- about how large the pile was, but in their testimony it was 300 people. And the Meja case stands out in my mind because after the fighting ended we went to Meja and conducted lengthy investigations. My colleague went there two days after the war ended, so that would be June 14th, and saw a few bodies by the side of the road exactly where the refugees had told us this incident had occurred, as well as remnants of personally identity documents and personal effects. And then I went to Meja in July and conducted lengthy interviews with villagers from the area, and it turned out that there were about 300 people missing from the village at that time and their testimony was very consistent, and it was very credible, and we -- I was -- I was particularly surprised at the level of corroboration between the witnesses in Kosovo and what we had heard in -- in Albania from the refugees. I remember that striking me. Of course there are other cases that I can talk about as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the interviews that you conducted. I mean, you said you went to Meja and spoke to people who were there about these allegations that you had heard from people streaming out of Kosovo earlier in April 1999. How were these interviews conducted? How long were the interviews in relation to -- now we're speaking only in relation to this specific incident of Meja.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, every interview was different, so I can't tell you that every single interview was the same way, no, that's not the case. But in general, we always strived to have these interviews be conducted in a one-on-one setting. They can take a long time, meaning two or three hours if not more. We do not ask leading questions. We try to have them tell us what they think is important and what is relevant, which includes the location and activities of the Kosovo Liberation Army or, in this period in question, the NATO forces, which of course were not on the ground but the air -- the air campaign from NATO. So, you know, whether that's the case for every interview I can't say, but that's certainly the goal to which we -- towards which we strive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify, when were you in Meja conducting this investigation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: July 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I would have to check my notes to be sure, but I was definitely in the Meja area for at least three days. Because, you know, the incident didn't just occur to the residents of Meja. There are a series of villages along this valley, and they all came through Meja; and Meja was the location of where the men were separated. So I visited at least three of those villages along this -- along this -- in this area. I also spent time in nearby Djakovica. Definitely I was there at least -- I was there definitely two days, and I believe three days in Djakovica and also in the nearby village called Kostajnica I think -- I think I'm confusing that with a certain politician. I'm sorry, I'm forgetting. Kosica maybe is the village, I'm sorry, I'm forgetting the name of that -- of that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you were conducting these investigations into the Meja incident, how did you go about trying to find persons who were able to provide information of what had occurred there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: You mean how did we identify the subjects for interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, the first question to ask is: Who was here at the day in question? And through that, the local villagers would tell you which individuals or which families were present at that time. I believe we also had the names of some of the people whom we had interviewed in Kukes from before and would have gone back to see those people. And through that - these are small, small towns - through that we would have identified people who said they had information to share about the incident in question. And then we would take those people and sit down with them in quiet and conduct the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you were there in July, were there residents or the villagers of Meja returning to the area? I mean, was it easy to locate persons who were able to speak about these events?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was very easy because by then virtually all, if not all, of the residents had returned to Kosovo. They came back almost immediately when the NATO campaign stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, while you were conducting these interviews in Meja, were you able to disturb any destruction to civilian property in the village?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In Meja itself? I'm sorry, I don't -- I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you spoke also about spending some days in Djakovica. Did you have the opportunity to visit the old district of Djakovica town?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to observe any sort of destruction to civilian property in that area?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, in the old town of Djakovica there was extensive destruction to homes and other civilian objects.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you explain what exactly you were able to see during the days that you were there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Most of the destruction I witnessed appeared to have come from fire, meaning it appeared as if the structures had been set on fire from inside. Again, that's because the walls were still standing and the wooden roofs had been burned as well as the charred remains of the interior of the homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you also interview persons, residents, of Djakovica to find out what had happened in the town during the period of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, yes I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall just generally what -- what sort of accounts people told of what had occurred there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, it was a chaotic scene because the town is fairly large, more than 150.000 people and lots of different incidents. But in general, Djakovica was one of the cities with the highest number of deaths. I think approximately 200 people died. And the witnesses told me that the Serbian security forces and Yugoslav security forces operated in a very coordinated manner. In particular, there were two distinct waves or what appeared to be operations, they said. One began very quickly after the NATO bombing started on March 24th and the other began on May 7th, each lasting for about a week. And they told me that security forces went through the city street by street in a systematic fashion rounding up individuals and expelling them from the city. There also appeared to have been an attempt to target some of the more prominent members of Djakovica, such as lawyers and doctors and politicians because a number of these individuals had been killed and witnesses told me that they had been taken into custody and -- and killed in the custody of security forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about hearing accounts of killings in the town of Djakovica. Is there any specific incident that you yourself investigated that sticks out in your mind that occurred in this town during the period we're speaking about in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, the incident that stands out most vividly in my memory happened on a street called Milos Gilic Street. There was an operation, what appeared to be a police operation according to the witnesses, to sweep through the street. And this was on the night of April 1st going into April 2nd. And a number of killings of civilians took place on that street but in particular it was one house, the address was 163 Milos Gilic Street in which 20 individuals from five different families had gathered, including, if memory serves me well, 12 children under the age of 16. And I interviewed two witnesses who saw security forces they claimed were police enter into this house. One of them talked about hearing shots and screams. And the 20 people in this house were killed and the inside of the house was set on fire. And I subsequently interviewed a member of the Gjakove city public works. I remember his name was Faton Polashku [phoen], and the authorities -- Serbian authorities had allowed him to work with his team to collect bodies throughout Djakovica during the time. And he told me that he entered the house at 163 Milos Gilic Street and retrieved the bodies, 20 bodies he said, which had been burned beyond recognition. I should add, this is not directly relevant to this incident but mentioning Faton Polashku reminds me, that he also testified to me that there had been many bodies buried in the Djakovica cemetery during this time and that at some point those bodies had been removed by Serbian forces. I interviewed separately and one-on-one a member of his staff who testified to the same. Neither of these men saw the removal themselves, but they had buried the bodies there and then the next day - this would have been I think it was in May, I would have to check the testimony to know exactly what time, I'm not certain on the day - that they came to the cemetery and saw that more than 70 bodies had been removed. And I visited the cemetery, Djakovica cemetery, in July and observed the dug-up earth in the cemetery and clear track marks from what looked like heavy machinery in the area where both of these men told me the bodies had been taken from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would these have been bodies of persons who had been killed during this offensive that you were describing during which a large number of persons were killed in Djakovica or had they been buried before this clean-up operation or sweep operation you spoke about took place?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: These were bodies of people who had been killed after March 24th when the NATO bombing began, had been buried by this crew, and then they were removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would these have been bodies of civilians or would these have been bodies of persons who were engaged in some sort of fighting or combat with security forces, based on what you were told?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Based on what I was told, the vast majority of them were civilians. I cannot exclude that some of them may have been fighters and there was also some fighting that did occur within Djakovica town. So some of those people may have been combatants. I can't testify that they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Abrahams, I think we have to stop for today because this is all the time we have, so we will have to continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. If that's a convenient moment, we will adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow in the morning. We must ask you to wait overnight, Mr. Abrahams, to continue at 9.00. The court officers will give you further assistance and directions before you leave tonight. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
